description: Uses second derivative of cumulative bid/ask depth across 5 orderbook levels as a volatility-regime filter. Concave curves (negative convexity = thick near top, thin at depth) indicate low uncertainty / strong consensus. In concave regimes, buy the token whose mid-price just dropped below its 6-snapshot rolling mean (mean-reversion fade). Skip convex regimes (uncertain markets).
hypothesis: Concave orderbook depth curves indicate market consensus and low uncertainty. Mean-reversion signals (price dipping below rolling mean) should be more reliable in these regimes compared to convex (uncertain) regimes.
analysis_notes: The convexity filter's apparent edge is fragile. Tighter thresholds systematically select cheaper tokens (avg entry drops from 0.457 baseline to 0.324 at thresh=-50 to 0.137 at thresh=-200). Win rate drops in lockstep (42% to 33% to 8%). The one positive-PnL threshold (-50) produces only $9.23 total profit on 269 trades ($0.034/trade) with a Sharpe of 0.018 and -$31 max drawdown. The 33% win rate is below random and the positive PnL comes from favorable payoff asymmetry on cheap tokens, not from predictive alpha. This is likely a statistical artifact at a single threshold rather than a robust signal.
next_steps: The convexity filter as implemented does not demonstrate reliable predictive power. The apparent edge at threshold=-50 is marginal ($0.034/trade, Sharpe 0.018) and likely driven by payoff asymmetry from buying cheap tokens rather than genuine regime detection. To validate: (1) test on full dataset to check if the threshold=-50 result persists, (2) control for entry price by comparing win rates at matched price levels with and without the convexity filter, (3) consider that the hypothesis may be fundamentally flawed - orderbook shape in binary prediction markets may not map to uncertainty regimes the same way it does in continuous markets.
